title: Before You Resist the Devil, There Is Something God Says You Must Do First
paragraphs: Before You Resist the Devil, There Is Something God Says You Must Do First
James 4:7 is often quoted as a battle cry against Satan. But the part we rush past may be the very reason we keep losing battles we desperately want to win.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” — James 4:7
Read it again.
Slowly.
Because there is an order here.
And the order matters.
Submit to God.
Then...
resist the devil.
Most of us love the second half.
We want to resist.
We want to rebuke.

We want the temptation gone, the oppression broken, the intrusive thoughts silenced, the old addiction defeated, the destructive relationship severed, the anger controlled, the lust extinguished, the fear conquered, the spiritual heaviness lifted.
We want to stand up and say, “Devil, get behind me.”
But James does not begin there.
Before Scripture tells you what to do about the devil, Scripture tells you what to do about God.
And that may expose something uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the battle we keep blaming entirely on the enemy is being prolonged by an area of our life we still refuse to surrender to the Lord.
James writes:
Ὑποτάγητε οὖν τῷ Θεῷ· ἀντίστητε δὲ τῷ διαβόλῳ, καὶ φεύξεται ἀφ’ ὑμῶν.
Hypotagēte oun tō Theō; antistēte de tō diabolō, kai pheuxetai aph’ hymōn.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
That first word matters.
Ὑποτάγητε — hypotagēte.
It carries the idea of placing oneself under, being subject to, yielding oneself to rightful authority.
James is not describing a casual acknowledgment that God exists.
He is describing surrender.
And surrender is where spiritual warfare begins.
That is difficult for us because we often want Jesus as Rescuer while quietly resisting Jesus as Lord.
We want Him to remove consequences without confronting choices.
We want peace without surrender.
Deliverance without repentance.
Victory without obedience.
Grace without transformation.
We want Christ to defeat what is destroying us while protecting the very thing through which destruction keeps entering.
But Jesus loves us too much to participate in that arrangement.
And maybe that is where this becomes personal.
You can resist the devil with your mouth while cooperating with temptation through your habits.
You can pray against darkness while secretly returning to what feeds it.
You can ask God to rescue your marriage while refusing to forgive.
You can ask Him to purify your mind while deliberately consuming what pollutes it.
You can ask Him to heal your heart while continuously reopening the wound.
You can ask Him for financial wisdom while refusing honesty and discipline.
You can ask Him to remove an ungodly relationship while keeping the messages you know you should delete.
You can worship publicly while protecting a private compromise.
You can know Christian vocabulary...
quote Scripture...
attend church...
raise your hands...
post Bible verses...
and still have one locked room in your heart where Jesus is standing at the door.
And you know exactly which room it is.
That is why James 4:7 cannot safely be separated from James 4.
James has been confronting quarrels, selfish desires, envy, worldly friendship and divided allegiance. He says that God “giveth more grace,” and then declares:
“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.” — James 4:6
Then comes the word:
Therefore.
Submit yourselves therefore to God.
In other words, James 4:7 is not an isolated spiritual-warfare formula.
It flows out of humility before God.
And immediately after telling believers to resist the devil, James continues:
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.” — James 4:8
Do you see it?
Submission.
Resistance.
Drawing near.
Cleansing.
Purification.
Humility.
James is describing a heart turning decisively toward God.
This is not magical language for making Satan disappear.
This is allegiance.
The Greek word translated “resist” is ἀντίστητε — antistēte.
It means to stand against, oppose, resist.
Not negotiate.
Not entertain.
Not see how close you can get without technically sinning.
Stand against.
There are moments when temptation arrives looking so familiar that you almost mistake it for yourself.
That old thought.
That old appetite.
That old bitterness.
That old website.
That old number.
That old fantasy.
That old rage.
That old need to be admired.
That old secret nobody knows.
And somewhere inside you comes the whisper:
Just once.
You deserve this.
Nobody will know.
You can repent afterward.
God understands.
And perhaps He does understand more deeply than you imagine.
But His understanding is not permission for the thing that is destroying you.
His grace is not permission to make peace with sin.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
The Gospel does not merely forgive the prisoner.
Jesus opens the prison door.
And sometimes we are standing in an open cell asking God why we still feel imprisoned while our hands remain wrapped around the bars.
That is why submission comes first.
Because biblical resistance is not fundamentally about how loudly you speak to Satan.
It is about whom you belong to.
Look at Jesus.
When Satan tempted Him in the wilderness, Christ did not bargain with temptation.
Again and again, He answered from Scripture.
“It is written...”
“It is written...”
“It is written...”
Jesus stood perfectly obedient to His Father.
And when Satan offered Him the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship, Christ answered:
“Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.” — Matthew 4:10
There it is again.
Allegiance.
Before spiritual warfare is about confrontation, it is about worship.
Who has your yes?
Who has your obedience?
Who gets the throne?
Because whatever sits on the throne of your heart will shape what you are willing to resist.
And this is where Christianity becomes far more uncomfortable than motivational religion.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your life.
He came as King.

The Gospel announces that the holy God against whom we have sinned did what we could never do for ourselves. Jesus Christ, truly righteous and without sin, bore sin at the cross and rose from the dead.
Our hope is not that we can submit perfectly enough to make God love us.
Our hope is Christ.
Our righteousness is not manufactured by spiritual discipline.
Our salvation is not earned by resisting temptation successfully.
We are saved by grace through faith.
Submission is not the price we pay to purchase grace.
Submission is the response of a heart that has encountered the King of grace.
And perhaps you have failed badly.
Maybe that is why these words hurt.
You knew better.
You promised God you would stop.
Then you went back.
You deleted it.
Then downloaded it again.
You walked away.
Then answered the message.
You forgave.
Then picked the bitterness back up.
You cried during worship Sunday...
and returned to the same secret Monday night.
Now shame has started preaching its own sermon to you:
God is tired of you.
You've ruined everything.
You're disgusting.
You're a hypocrite.
You might as well stop trying.
But listen carefully.
That voice is not the Gospel.
The Gospel does not say sin is insignificant.
The Gospel says sin was so serious that Christ went to a cross...
and grace is so astonishing that the cross can save sinners like us.
Peter had a scandal.
David had a scandal.
The woman at the well carried a history she could not rewrite.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left with which to repair his reputation.
Paul had blood in his biography.
Yet none of their stories ended at their worst chapter.
That does not make their sins beautiful.
It makes Christ beautiful.
This is what grace does.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace walks into darkness and brings sinners into the light.
Grace does not say, “Stay exactly as you are.”
Grace says, “Come.”
Grace forgives.
Grace cleanses.
Grace restores.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
And when you fall, the answer is not to hide farther from God.
James says:
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.”
Come back.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel spiritual again.
Not after you have punished yourself sufficiently.
Come back now.
Confess honestly.
Repent genuinely.
Bring the hidden thing into His light.
Put the relationship under His authority.
Put your sexuality under His authority.
Put your money under His authority.
Put your ambition under His authority.
Put your wounds under His authority.
Put your phone under His authority.
Put your entertainment under His authority.
Put your anger under His authority.
Put your future under His authority.
Put the thing you are most afraid to surrender...
under His authority.
Then resist.
When temptation says, “Come back,” resist.
When shame says, “Run from God,” resist.
When bitterness says, “Never forgive,” resist.
When pride says, “You don't need correction,” resist.
When lust says, “Nobody will know,” resist.
When despair says, “Nothing will ever change,” resist.
When the enemy twists God's character, resist him with truth.
But do not misunderstand the promise.
“He will flee from you” does not mean Christians will never face temptation again.
Even Jesus experienced repeated temptation. Scripture calls believers to remain watchful because the Christian life involves ongoing spiritual conflict.
James is teaching us where we stand.
Under God.
Against the devil.
There is an enormous difference between those positions.
We do not stand over God and ask Him to bless our agenda.
We stand under His authority.
We do not stand under Satan's accusations as condemned prisoners.
In Christ, we stand against him.
And perhaps the most important question you can ask tonight is not:
“How do I make the devil flee?”
Perhaps it is:
“Jesus, what have I still not surrendered to You?”
Don't answer too quickly.
Sit with it.
Maybe a name came into your mind.
A habit.
A wound.
A screen.
A relationship.
A grudge.
A secret.
A dream you have decided God is not allowed to touch.
That may be where today's battle begins.
Not with shouting.
With surrender.
“Lord Jesus, this belongs to You.”
Sometimes the strongest spiritual-warrior prayer is spoken through tears.
“I don't want to give this up...
but I want You more.”
That is surrender.
Not the absence of struggle.
The transfer of authority.
And if you fail again, do not turn failure into your identity.
Run to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Stand again.
Resistance is not pretending temptation has disappeared.
Resistance is refusing to crown it king.
Jesus is King.
Maybe someone reading this has been exhausted because you have spent years fighting symptoms while protecting the root.
Today can be different.
Not because you suddenly became stronger.
Because surrender finally brought the battle into its proper order.
Submit to God.
Resist the devil.
And he will flee from you.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you also do not have to keep pretending.
Someone else reading those words may realize they are not the only believer fighting a battle behind a smile.
Not because you need another post sitting in a collection, but because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions difficult to remember tomorrow.
Come back to James 4.
Come back to surrender.
Come back to Christ.
And think of one person right now who has been fighting quietly.

Someone scrolling tonight may never tell you what they are battling. They may never tell you that the words you shared reached them five minutes before they were about to return to something that had nearly destroyed them.
We cannot manufacture what God will do with something shared in faithfulness.
But we can refuse to keep biblical encouragement to ourselves.
Supporting Gospel work financially does not purchase God's favor, make anyone more righteous, or prove that someone loves God more than another believer. Christ alone is our boast.
But generosity can be one genuine way believers steward what God has entrusted to them.
Not because sharing a post earns heaven.
Not because an algorithm is the mission.
Jesus is the mission.
If this truth helped you, help put it where another wounded, tempted, ashamed, exhausted person might encounter it.
Follow for daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment.
And comment something honest.
“Jesus, I surrender.”
Because maybe your greatest breakthrough will not begin the moment you finally become strong enough to fight harder.
Maybe it begins the moment you finally stop fighting God for the throne.
